barriers.description: Clinical encounter routines and opening questions caused information about patients' life context to emerge haphazardly, limiting researchers' ability to observe natural disclosures in clinic visits.
barriers.justification: This organizational/human-environment constraint hindered designers' ability to manage user understanding and to study the context of use because relevant life information did not surface reliably during observations.
barriers.reference_excerpt: First, information about patients’ capacity and context sometimes arose naturally, but haphazardly throughout the visit. Patients who spoke freely and enjoyed talking about their life upon meeting them, changed completely during the encounter. There, they spoke only of their medical conditions and immediate concerns, and none of the life issues they had mentioned to us previously.

barriers.description: Existing assessment data (questionnaires) completed by patients were not reviewed or discussed in encounters, preventing designers from using those data to inform understanding.
barriers.justification: Because completed assessments were ignored in practice, researchers could not rely on them to specify user requirements or understand context of use, limiting their ability to integrate feedback into design decisions.
barriers.reference_excerpt: Assessments that offered insights about the patient’s capacity were not used for this purpose. For example, in one encounter, the patient had filled out multiple questionnaires, one regarding depression, one regarding anxiety, and one regarding alcohol consumption. Despite being available during the encounter, these were never reviewed or discussed.

barriers.description: Patient advisory group members initially found the concept of clinicians asking about coping unfamiliar, which limited their immediate engagement with the design idea.
barriers.justification: This lack of familiarity among users hindered designers' ability to facilitate user involvement and to manage user understanding during co-design activities, requiring additional effort to introduce and explain the concept.
barriers.reference_excerpt: At first, participants struggled with this concept; it was clearly foreign to them, even after years of living with chronic conditions.

barriers.description: The terminology researchers initially used to describe patient capacity was more suitable to researchers and clinicians than to patients, necessitating rewording to enable patient participation.
barriers.justification: This communication/terminology mismatch impeded designers' ability to facilitate user involvement and to specify user requirements until language was made patient-friendly.
barriers.reference_excerpt: The words that we used to describe patient capacity (Physical, Emotional, Personal, Financial, Social, and Environmental) were friendlier to researchers and physicians than to patients. To fully allow patients to participate, these needed to be reconsidered.

barriers.description: Older patients struggled with the prototypes' color contrast, forcing designers to change the visual design to a high-contrast black-and-white version.
barriers.justification: This usability/accessibility issue required designers to revise design solutions and iterate further, directly affecting the produce design solutions and integrate feedback & iteration workloads.
barriers.reference_excerpt: We learned from stakeholder feedback, that older patients struggled with the color contrast and preferred a highly contrasted, black-and-white version.
